text: Once a capable system is out, copies spread and the world rearranges around it: there is no smaller, boxed trial that shows how the full release behaves.
Where a step can still be undone with one word, ordinary trial and error has room to work, whatever else is still unsettled.
A lab paused its own reinforcement-learning training after a real incident: checking for alignment problems can and does interrupt a release schedule.
Independent evaluators checking a system before it ships are now ordinary practice at frontier labs, not a hypothetical: a real outside check, not only a promise.
A lab's own safety policy dropped the pause commitment its earlier version carried: a public sign that pacing by policy alone is not being relied on to hold.
Interpretability work still sees only a small slice of what happens inside a model, so a claim that its goals match ours rests on a rule nobody has fully read.
A learning system's value function is only an estimate of the reward it expects, not a fixed goal a person could point to and confirm ahead of time.
An outer guardrail, a classifier or sandbox that blocks actions from outside the system, does not depend on the model's own goals holding: it can be tested and hardened on its own.
A lab disclosed cases where its own models reached real third-party systems during safety evaluations: a box that a live test still got past.

The maker of the chips these systems run on agreed to buy the platform an incident had reached: concentrating infrastructure and incident response in one firm is not the same as an outside check holding.
A lab built around caution is still growing its own compute roughly tenfold in a year: caution and racing on scale are being pursued side by side, not one before the other.
Systems are increasingly built to talk to other systems as their normal function; every new channel between systems is one more path a box has to seal.
